bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.title: Alignment, BLAST & Structure Tools
kp: Global = Needleman–Wunsch (1970); local = Smith–Waterman (1981); both use dynamic programming.
Scoring: match/mismatch (DNA); PAM and BLOSUM (proteins); linear or affine gap penalties.
Identity and similarity are percentages; homology is shared ancestry (orthologues vs paralogues).
MSA: progressive using a guide tree (Clustal); iterative (MUSCLE, MAFFT).
BLAST (Altschul, 1990): words → seeds → HSP extension → E-value / bit score.
blastn, blastp, blastx, tblastn, tblastx.
FASTA (Lipman and Pearson, 1985): k-tuple diagonals, rescoring, banded SW.
RasMol and Swiss-PdbViewer display PDB coordinates; Swiss-PdbViewer also models and superimposes.
Bioinformatics applies to genomics, proteomics, drug design, medicine, agriculture and evolution.

sa.q: Differentiate global and local alignment.
sa.a: Global (NW) aligns entire sequences and suits similar sequences of similar length. Local (SW) aligns only the best-matching regions and suits divergent sequences or shared domains.

sa.q: What are PAM and BLOSUM matrices?
sa.a: Substitution matrices giving scores for replacing one amino acid with another. PAM is based on an evolutionary model of point accepted mutations; BLOSUM is derived from conserved blocks of related proteins (BLOSUM62 is the default).

sa.q: Explain how BLAST works.
sa.a: The query is split into words, matching words (seeds) are found in the database, seeds are extended in both directions to form HSPs, and significance is expressed as bit score and E-value.

sa.q: List the BLAST programs.
sa.a: blastn, blastp, blastx, tblastn and tblastx, differing in the type of query and database and use of translation.

sa.q: Compare BLAST and FASTA.
sa.a: Both are heuristic similarity searches. BLAST uses word hits and extension to HSPs and is faster; FASTA uses k-tuple diagonals followed by rescoring and a banded Smith–Waterman, and can be more sensitive at small ktup.

sa.q: What is multiple sequence alignment and name two tools?
sa.a: Alignment of three or more sequences to reveal conserved residues, done progressively using a guide tree. Tools: Clustal Omega, MUSCLE, MAFFT, T-Coffee.

sa.q: Name two protein structure visualising tools and their uses.
sa.a: RasMol (fast display in wireframe, spacefill, cartoon styles) and Swiss-PdbViewer (analysis, superposition, mutation and homology modelling).

sa.q: State four applications of bioinformatics.
sa.a: Genome annotation, drug discovery (docking), personalised medicine, evolutionary analysis/phylogeny, crop improvement.

gl.d: Arrangement of sequences to show similarity.
A position in an alignment representing an insertion or deletion.
Method that solves a problem by combining optimal solutions to sub-problems.
Point Accepted Mutation matrices from evolutionary models.
Block Substitution Matrix derived from conserved protein blocks.
High-scoring Segment Pair: a local alignment reported by BLAST.
Expected number of chance hits with the same or better score.
Normalised alignment score independent of scoring matrix.
The sequence you submit for a database search.
Tree that decides the order of progressive alignment.
Text file of atomic coordinates of a macromolecule.
A sequence sharing common ancestry with another.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.title: Fundamentals of Biotechnology — Definition, Scope & Importance
kp: Biotechnology is the application of biological organisms, systems, or processes to make products or modify processes for specific use (UN CBD definition, 1992).
The term Biotechnology was coined by Hungarian engineer Károly Ereky in 1919.
Traditional biotechnology includes fermentation (bread, wine, beer, cheese). Modern biotechnology involves rDNA technology, PCR, CRISPR — post-1953 era.
Branches: Red (Medical), Green (Agricultural), White (Industrial), Blue (Marine), Yellow (Food), Grey (Environmental) biotechnology.
rDNA technology tools: Restriction endonucleases (scissors), DNA ligase (glue), plasmids (vectors), E. coli (host) — first demonstrated by Cohen & Boyer, 1973.
First recombinant protein produced commercially: Human insulin (Humulin) by Eli Lilly & Genentech, 1982, using E. coli.
PCR — invented by Kary Mullis (1983, Nobel 1993). Amplifies specific DNA in vitro using thermal cycling; enzyme: Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus.
Bt cotton contains cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis; produces Bt toxin that kills bollworm. Approved in India in 2002; covers >95% cotton area.
Golden Rice — biofortified with β-carotene (pro-Vitamin A) using psy and crtI genes. Developed by Potrykus & Beyer (1999) to combat Vitamin A deficiency.
Monoclonal antibodies — produced by hybridoma technology (Kohler & Milstein, 1975; Nobel 1984). Single clone B cells + myeloma cells → hybridoma → MAb.
Dolly the sheep (1996) — first mammal cloned from adult somatic cell by Ian Wilmut. Proved somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) can reprogram differentiated cells.
CRISPR-Cas9 — genome editing tool derived from bacterial immune system; guide RNA directs Cas9 nuclease to target. Nobel Prize 2020 to Jennifer Doudna & Emmanuelle Charpentier.
Bioremediation — using microorganisms to degrade pollutants. Pseudomonas putida (first GMO patent by Chakrabarty, 1980) degrades petroleum hydrocarbons.
Totipotency — every plant cell can regenerate a complete organism (Haberlandt, 1902). Basis of plant tissue culture — micropropagation, somatic hybridisation.

sa.q: Define biotechnology. Who coined the term?
sa.a: Biotechnology is the application of biological organisms, systems, or processes to make or modify products and processes for specific use (CBD, 1992). It integrates biology with technology to develop solutions for medicine, agriculture, industry, and environment. The term was coined by Hungarian engineer Károly Ereky in 1919.

sa.q: Distinguish between Traditional and Modern Biotechnology with examples.
sa.a: Traditional biotechnology uses natural organisms without genetic manipulation for processes like fermentation (bread, wine, cheese, yoghurt) over thousands of years. Modern biotechnology (post-1953) employs recombinant DNA technology, PCR, CRISPR, and genetic engineering to precisely modify organisms. Examples: Traditional — beer brewing using yeast; Modern — production of human insulin using E. coli with inserted human insulin gene.

sa.q: What are restriction enzymes? Give their role in rDNA technology.
sa.a: Restriction endonucleases are bacterial enzymes that recognise and cut specific palindromic DNA sequences. They act as "molecular scissors." In rDNA technology, restriction enzymes cut the desired gene from the donor DNA and also cut the vector (plasmid) at the same recognition sequence, creating compatible sticky ends that allow the gene to be inserted into the vector. Example: EcoRI cuts at 5′-GAATTC-3′ sequence. Werner Arber, Nathans & H. Smith won the Nobel Prize in 1978 for their discovery.

sa.q: What is bioremediation? Name two microorganisms used in it.
sa.a: Bioremediation is the use of living organisms (mainly bacteria and fungi) to degrade, detoxify, or neutralise hazardous pollutants in the environment into harmless substances like CO₂ and H₂O. It is cost-effective, eco-friendly, and produces no secondary pollutants. Two microorganisms: (1) Pseudomonas putida — degrades petroleum hydrocarbons (oil spills); (2) Thiobacillus ferrooxidans — used in biomining to extract copper and gold from low-grade ores.

sa.q: Explain the significance of Bt cotton in India.
sa.a: Bt cotton contains the cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis which produces Bt toxin (Cry proteins). This toxin forms pores in the gut of bollworm larvae (Helicoverpa armigera) causing death, while being harmless to mammals. Approved in India in 2002, Bt cotton now covers over 95% of India's cotton acreage. Its significance: (a) Reduced pesticide use by ~50%; (b) Increased yield by 30–40%; (c) Reduced production costs for farmers; (d) Decreased pesticide-related health hazards. Concern: resistance development in pests over time requires refuge zones.

sa.q: Write short notes on monoclonal antibodies and their applications.
sa.a: Monoclonal antibodies (MAbs) are identical antibodies produced by a single clone of B lymphocytes (hybridoma cells) and are highly specific to one antigen. Hybridoma technology was developed by Kohler & Milstein (1975), earning the Nobel Prize in 1984. Process: Immunise animal → B cells + myeloma cells → hybridoma → single clone → MAb. Applications: (1) Cancer therapy — Herceptin (breast cancer), Rituximab (lymphoma); (2) Autoimmune diseases — Adalimumab (Humira); (3) Transplant rejection prevention; (4) Diagnostics — pregnancy test kits, COVID-19 rapid tests, HIV tests; (5) Research — Western blot, ELISA, flow cytometry.

sa.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9? Why is it considered a revolutionary tool?
sa.a: CRISPR-Cas9 (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats — CRISPR-associated protein 9) is a revolutionary genome editing technology derived from a bacterial immune defence system. A guide RNA (gRNA) directs the Cas9 nuclease to a specific target DNA sequence, where it makes a precise double-strand cut. The cell's repair mechanism can then introduce desired changes. It is revolutionary because: (a) Highly precise — single base editing possible; (b) Simple to design; (c) Fast and affordable compared to previous tools (ZFN, TALEN); (d) Works in any organism. Jennifer Doudna & Emmanuelle Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020.

sa.q: Write the importance of biotechnology in healthcare.
sa.a: Biotechnology's role in healthcare includes: (1) Therapeutic proteins — Human insulin, growth hormone, clotting factors, erythropoietin produced via rDNA technology; (2) Vaccines — Hepatitis B vaccine (yeast), HPV vaccine, COVID-19 mRNA vaccine (Moderna, Pfizer); (3) Monoclonal antibodies — targeted cancer therapy, autoimmune disease treatment; (4) Gene therapy — correcting defective genes in SCID, haemophilia, β-thalassaemia; (5) Diagnostics — PCR (disease detection), ELISA (hormone levels, pregnancy), DNA fingerprinting (forensics); (6) Stem cell therapy — regenerating damaged tissues; (7) Pharmacogenomics — personalised drug treatment based on individual genetic profile.

gl.d: The application of biological organisms, systems, or processes to develop products and processes for specific uses in medicine, agriculture, industry, and the environment. Coined by Károly Ereky (1919).
A hybrid DNA molecule formed by combining DNA sequences from two different organisms using restriction enzymes and DNA ligase. The foundation of modern genetic engineering.
A bacterial enzyme that cuts double-stranded DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences. Acts as "molecular scissors" in rDNA technology. Example: EcoRI, BamHI.
A small, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA molecule in bacteria that replicates independently. Used as a vector (vehicle) to carry and express foreign genes in host organisms.
A technique for amplifying specific DNA sequences in vitro using thermal cycling (denaturation → annealing → extension). Uses Taq polymerase. Invented by Kary Mullis (1983).
An organism whose genome has been altered using genetic engineering techniques, introducing genes from another species. Examples: Bt cotton, Golden Rice, recombinant E. coli.
Highly specific antibodies produced by a single clone of hybridoma cells, all identical and targeting one specific antigen. Used in cancer therapy, diagnostics, and immunotherapy.
A therapeutic approach involving introduction, alteration, or replacement of a defective gene in a patient's cells to treat inherited or acquired diseases (e.g., SCID, haemophilia).
The use of microorganisms or plants to degrade, neutralise, or transform pollutants in contaminated soil, water, or air into harmless substances. Eco-friendly and cost-effective clean-up technology.
A DNA molecule (plasmid, phage, BAC) used as a vehicle to carry a foreign gene into a host cell where it can be replicated and expressed. Must have ori, MCS, selectable marker.

A bacterial-derived genome editing system using guide RNA to direct Cas9 nuclease to precise DNA locations for targeted cuts. Revolutionary for gene therapy, crop improvement, and research. Nobel 2020.
Microbial anaerobic breakdown of organic compounds (sugars) to produce energy, alcohol, acids, or gases. Used industrially to produce ethanol, antibiotics, vitamins, enzymes, and dairy products.
The ability of a single plant cell to regenerate a complete organism because it contains the entire genetic information. The fundamental principle underlying plant tissue culture (Haberlandt, 1902).
A controlled vessel providing optimal conditions (temperature, pH, O₂, agitation) for large-scale microbial cultivation to produce industrial products like enzymes, antibiotics, or biofuels.
An organism that carries a foreign gene (transgene) from another species in its genome. The transgene is heritable and expressed in all cells. Examples: Transgenic mice, Bt cotton, Dolly (cloned).
Undifferentiated cells capable of self-renewal and differentiation into any cell type. Embryonic stem cells (pluripotent) and adult stem cells have therapeutic applications in regenerative medicine.

blotting_techniques.html.title: Blotting Techniques
kp: Southern blot (E. M. Southern, 1975) → DNA; Northern → RNA; Western → protein.
Gel → membrane transfer preserves the band pattern; probes then locate the target.
Southern and Northern blots rely on nucleic acid hybridisation; Western relies on antigen–antibody binding.
Southern: DNA is denatured with alkali. Northern: formaldehyde gel, no alkali, RNase-free.
Membranes: nylon/nitrocellulose for nucleic acids; nitrocellulose/PVDF for proteins.
Transfer: capillary (Southern/Northern) versus electroblotting (Western).
Blocking reduces background; stringency is raised by high temperature and low salt.
Uses: transgene confirmation, RFLP, DNA fingerprinting (Southern); gene expression (Northern); HIV confirmation, recombinant protein (Western).

sa.q: What is blotting? Name the three types.
sa.a: Blotting is the transfer of electrophoretically separated DNA, RNA or protein from a gel to a membrane, followed by detection with a labelled probe. The three types are Southern (DNA), Northern (RNA) and Western (protein).

sa.q: Describe the steps of Southern blotting.
sa.a: Restriction digestion of DNA → agarose gel electrophoresis → depurination and alkali denaturation → capillary transfer to nitrocellulose/nylon membrane → fixation by UV or baking → prehybridisation (blocking) → hybridisation with labelled probe → washing → autoradiographic detection.

sa.q: How does Northern blotting differ from Southern blotting?
sa.a: Northern detects RNA; the gel is denaturing (formaldehyde), alkali is not used because it hydrolyses RNA, and RNase-free conditions are essential. It shows transcript size and level of expression.

sa.q: Explain the principle of Western blotting.
sa.a: Proteins separated by SDS-PAGE are electroblotted onto a membrane, blocked, and probed with a specific primary antibody. An enzyme-linked secondary antibody binds the primary antibody and generates a visible or chemiluminescent signal at the position of the target protein.

sa.q: What is stringency in hybridisation?
sa.a: Stringency is the strictness of conditions that determine how closely a probe must match its target to remain bound. High temperature and low salt give high stringency and fewer false positives.

sa.q: Write two applications of Western blotting.
sa.a: (1) Confirmatory test for HIV infection; (2) confirming expression and size of a recombinant protein in a host cell.

gl.d: Transfer of separated biomolecules from a gel to a membrane for detection.
A labelled single-stranded nucleic acid (or antibody) that binds a specific target.
Base pairing between a probe and its complementary target sequence.
How demanding the washing/hybridisation conditions are; high stringency requires near-perfect matches.
Moving molecules from gel to membrane by buffer drawn up through absorbent paper.
Transfer of proteins out of a gel to a membrane using an electric field.
Protein or DNA solution (milk, BSA, Denhardt's) that covers free membrane sites.
Antibody that recognises the target protein.
Enzyme-conjugated antibody that recognises the primary antibody.
Detection of radioactive signal using X-ray film.
Polyvinylidene difluoride: a membrane that binds proteins strongly.
A constitutively expressed gene (e.g. GAPDH) used as a loading control.
Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats — natural bacterial immune sequences repurposed for gene editing.
A nuclease enzyme (protein) with two cutting domains (HNH, RuvC) that creates a double-strand break in DNA at the target site.
A ~20-nucleotide RNA designed to be complementary to the target DNA sequence; directs Cas9 to the correct genomic location.
Protospacer Adjacent Motif (5′-NGG-3′ for SpCas9) — a short DNA sequence immediately next to the target; required for Cas9 binding and cutting.
The specific DNA sequence in the genome that the gRNA is designed to match and that Cas9 will cut.
A cut in both strands of the DNA double helix, created by Cas9 at the target location.
Non-Homologous End Joining — a fast but error-prone DNA repair pathway that introduces indels at the break site, disrupting gene function.
Homology-Directed Repair — a precise DNA repair pathway that uses a provided donor template to introduce an exact sequence at the break site.
Disruption or inactivation of a gene, typically achieved via NHEJ-mediated indels that cause a frameshift mutation.
Unintended editing at genomic sites with sequences similar to the intended target — a key safety concern in clinical use.
Modification of reproductive cells (egg, sperm, embryo) — changes are heritable and passed to future generations; ethically restricted.
Insertions and/or deletions introduced at the cut site by NHEJ repair; often cause frameshift mutations that disrupt the reading frame.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.title: Enzymes in Genetic Engineering – Interactive Learning App

gl.d: A double-stranded DNA sequence in which both strands read identically in the 5' to 3' direction; the basis for restriction enzyme recognition.
Short single-stranded nucleotide overhangs produced by staggered restriction enzyme cuts. Also called cohesive ends. They can hydrogen-bond with complementary sequences for ligation.
Fully double-stranded DNA ends with no overhangs, produced when a restriction enzyme cuts both strands at the same position within the recognition sequence.
An enzyme that catalyzes formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH of one DNA strand and the 5'-phosphate of another, joining two DNA fragments.
A DNA molecule (e.g., plasmid, bacteriophage, cosmid) used to carry a foreign DNA fragment into a host cell for replication and/or expression.
The process of inserting a DNA fragment into a vector, introducing it into a host cell, and allowing the host to replicate, producing many identical copies of the DNA.
A specific short DNA sequence (usually 4 to 8 bp, palindromic) that is recognized and bound by a restriction endonuclease before cleavage of the DNA.
Complementary DNA. Synthesized from an mRNA template by reverse transcriptase. Represents only the exon sequences (coding regions) with no introns.
DNA molecule formed by combining DNA sequences from two or more different organisms or sources, typically a gene of interest inserted into a cloning vector.
Addition of a methyl group to specific bases in DNA. Bacteria methylate their own restriction sites to protect their DNA from self-cleavage by their own restriction enzymes.
Introduction of foreign DNA (e.g., recombinant plasmid) into a bacterial cell. Successful transformants are selected using antibiotic resistance or other selectable markers.
A technique used to characterize a DNA molecule by cutting it with various restriction enzymes and analyzing fragment sizes to determine the positions of restriction sites on the DNA.

gene_therapy_app.html.title: Gene Therapy – Ex Vivo & In Vivo

gl.d: Medical approach using therapeutic genes to treat or prevent disease by correcting genetic abnormalities in patient cells.
Latin for "outside the living." Gene modification occurs outside the patient's body in a lab setting before cells are returned.
Latin for "within the living." Gene delivery occurs directly inside the patient's body without removing cells.
A carrier (usually viral) used to deliver therapeutic genetic material into target cells.
A functional copy of a gene introduced into patient cells to compensate for a defective or missing gene.
The specific cell type into which the therapeutic gene is introduced to produce the desired effect.
A gene (e.g., p53) that normally restrains cell growth; when mutated, can lead to cancer.
A permanent change in the DNA sequence of a gene, which may disrupt normal protein function.
Adeno-Associated Virus — a small, non-pathogenic virus widely used as a vector in approved gene therapies.
An ex vivo approach where T-lymphocytes are engineered with chimeric antigen receptors to target and destroy cancer cells.
Gene modification of body (non-reproductive) cells; changes are not heritable by offspring.
A risk where a retroviral vector integrates near a proto-oncogene, potentially activating cancer-causing pathways.

hgp_ethics_ipr.html.title: Human Genome Project, Ethics & IPR
kp: HGP: 1990–2003; ~3.1 Gb; ~20,000 genes; <2% coding; ~99.9% similarity between individuals.
Public consortium (clone-by-clone, BAC) versus Celera (whole-genome shotgun); T2T gapless genome in 2022.
Maps: genetic (cM), cytogenetic (bands), physical (bp), sequence map.
Applications: disease genes, pharmacogenomics, forensics, evolution, bioinformatics.
ELSI accounted for 3–5% of the HGP budget.
Ethics: privacy, consent, discrimination, germline editing, GM food, animal welfare, equity.
India: GEAC, RCGM, IBSC; EPA 1986/Rules 1989; Biological Diversity Act 2002; PPV&FR Act 2001.
Patent criteria: novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability; TRIPS: 20 years; Budapest Treaty for microbes.
Section 3(j) of Indian Patents Act excludes plants and animals; neem and turmeric patents revoked.

sa.q: What is the Human Genome Project? State its goals.
sa.a: An international project (1990–2003) to sequence the ~3 billion base pairs of the human genome, identify its genes, store data in databases, develop analysis tools, and study the ethical, legal and social implications.

sa.q: Differentiate genetic and physical maps.
sa.a: A genetic map is based on recombination frequency (cM) between markers; a physical map shows actual distance in base pairs using restriction sites, STS and clone contigs.

sa.q: Compare the public and Celera approaches.
sa.a: The public consortium used hierarchical clone-by-clone BAC sequencing guided by maps; Celera used whole-genome shotgun sequencing followed by computer assembly.

sa.q: List four applications of HGP.
sa.a: Identification of disease genes, predictive testing and pharmacogenomics, forensic DNA profiling, comparative genomics/evolution, development of bioinformatics.

sa.q: What are the ethical issues related to genetic information?
sa.a: Privacy, discrimination by insurers/employers, informed consent, genetic testing of minors, germline editing, access and equity.

sa.q: What is a patent? What are the criteria for patentability?
sa.a: A patent is an exclusive right for 20 years to an inventor in exchange for disclosure. The invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable.

sa.q: What is biopiracy? Give an example.
sa.a: Unauthorised exploitation of biological resources or traditional knowledge without benefit sharing. Example: the patents on neem and turmeric, later revoked.

gl.d: The complete set of DNA of an organism.
A set of overlapping DNA fragments forming a continuous sequence.
Bacterial artificial chromosome, a vector carrying 100–200 kb inserts.
Sequence-tagged site: short unique DNA sequence used as a map landmark.
Single nucleotide polymorphism: a single-base difference between individuals.
Ethical, Legal and Social Implications of genomics research.
Voluntary agreement after understanding risks and benefits.
Exclusive right to an invention for a fixed period (20 years).
WTO agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights.
Unauthorised commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge.
Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, India's regulator of GMO release.
Tag for products with qualities linked to their region of origin.

hybridoma_monoclonal_antibodies.html.title: Hybridoma & Monoclonal Antibodies
kp: Hybridoma = B lymphocyte + myeloma cell; Köhler & Milstein, 1975; Nobel 1984.
Myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient; HAT medium selects hybrids.
Fusing agent: PEG. Screening: ELISA. Cloning: limiting dilution.
Mouse antibodies cause HAMA; solution: chimeric (-ximab), humanised (-zumab), human (-umab).
Phage display (Smith and Winter, Nobel 2018) produces fully human MAbs.
Uses: cancer therapy, autoimmune disease, diagnostics, purification, research.

sa.q: What are monoclonal antibodies? How are they different from polyclonal antibodies?
sa.a: MAbs are identical antibodies from a single B-cell clone, specific for one epitope. Polyclonal antibodies come from many clones and recognise many epitopes.

sa.q: Describe the production of monoclonal antibodies.
sa.a: Immunise mouse → collect spleen B cells → fuse with HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells using PEG → select hybridomas in HAT medium → screen supernatants by ELISA → clone by limiting dilution → large-scale culture or ascites → purification.

sa.q: Explain the role of HAT medium.
sa.a: Aminopterin blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis, so cells must use the HGPRT salvage pathway with hypoxanthine and thymidine. HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells die, B cells die naturally, and hybridomas survive.

sa.q: Give four applications of MAbs.
sa.a: Cancer therapy (trastuzumab, rituximab); diagnosis (pregnancy test, ELISA); immunoaffinity purification; prevention of graft rejection (OKT3); imaging.

sa.q: Why are humanised antibodies preferred?
sa.a: They reduce the HAMA response, have longer half-lives and are safer for repeated administration.

gl.d: Y-shaped protein that binds a specific antigen.
The part of an antigen recognised by an antibody.
Immortal antibody-secreting cell formed by B cell and myeloma fusion.
Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine medium that selects hybridomas.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase, enzyme of the salvage pathway.
Fluid in the mouse peritoneum that accumulates MAb-secreting hybridoma cells.
Complementarity-determining region of the antibody variable domain.
Human anti-mouse antibody immune response.
Technique displaying peptides or antibody fragments on phage for selection.
Constant tail of an antibody that engages immune effector functions.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.title: Industrial Biotechnology — Fermentation & Ethanol Production
kp: Industrial Biotechnology (White Biotechnology) applies microorganisms/enzymes for large-scale manufacture of chemicals, fuels, food, and pharmaceuticals.
Fermentation is the microbial anaerobic breakdown of organic compounds (sugars) to produce energy, alcohol, acids, or gases.
The principle is NAD⁺ regeneration: NADH produced in glycolysis is re-oxidised by reducing pyruvate to ethanol or lactate, allowing continuous glycolysis.
Key enzyme for alcoholic fermentation: Pyruvate decarboxylase (pyruvate → acetaldehyde) and Alcohol dehydrogenase (acetaldehyde → ethanol + NAD⁺).
Net equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + 2 ATP (Gay-Lussac; yield = 51.1 g ethanol per 100 g glucose).
Optimal conditions for yeast fermentation: Temperature 28–32°C; pH 4.5–5.5; sugar concentration 10–18°Brix; anaerobic; nutrients (N, P, Mg).
Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the preferred organism for ethanol production — facultative anaerobe, ethanol-tolerant (up to 14–15%), GRAS, high yield, well-characterised genome.
Raw materials: Molasses (cheapest; 50–55% sucrose), Sugarcane juice (direct), Starch sources (corn, wheat — require saccharification by amylase).
Ethanol production steps: Raw material prep → Sterilisation → Inoculation → Fermentation (28–32°C, 24–72 h) → Distillation (78.4°C) → Rectification (95–96%) → Dehydration (≥99.5%).
95–96% ethanol = azeotropic (cannot be purified further by simple distillation). Molecular sieves or azeotropic distillation needed for anhydrous (fuel-grade) ethanol.
Aerobic fermentation (O₂ present): high ATP yield, products = CO₂ + H₂O + biomass; used for antibiotics, citric acid, enzymes. Anaerobic: 2 ATP, products = ethanol or lactic acid.
Product inhibition: Ethanol >14–15% v/v inhibits yeast. This limits single-batch ethanol concentration, requiring distillation for concentration.
Applications of ethanol: Biofuel (E10, E20 blending), antiseptic (70%), solvent, chemical feedstock (acetaldehyde, ethyl acetate), beverages, pharmaceutical solvent.
India's Ethanol Programme: National Biofuel Policy (2018) targets 20% ethanol blending in petrol (E20) by 2025–26, primarily using molasses and damaged food grains.

gl.d: The microbial metabolic process of partial anaerobic breakdown of organic compounds (sugars) to produce energy, alcohol, organic acids, or gases without the net consumption of oxygen.
The starting material or carbon source (e.g., glucose, sucrose, starch, molasses) that microorganisms use as food and energy source during fermentation.
A small quantity of active starter culture of the desired microorganism added to a fermentation medium to initiate the fermentation process.
A controlled vessel or tank designed to provide optimal physical and chemical conditions (temperature, pH, aeration) for large-scale microbial growth and product synthesis.
The most widely used yeast in industrial fermentation. Also called baker's yeast or brewer's yeast; converts sugars to ethanol + CO₂ under anaerobic conditions. GRAS status.
The first stage of sugar metabolism occurring in the cytoplasm, converting one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate molecules (3C) with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
The enzyme complex in yeast responsible for alcoholic fermentation. Includes key enzymes like pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. Discovered by Eduard Buchner (1897).
The enzyme that catalyses the final step of alcoholic fermentation: reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH, thereby regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis.
A thick dark syrup by-product of sugar refining containing 45–55% fermentable sugars. The cheapest and most commonly used substrate for industrial ethanol fermentation.
The enzymatic hydrolysis of starch or cellulose into fermentable sugars (glucose, maltose) using amylase or cellulase enzymes as a preparatory step before fermentation.
A separation technique using differences in boiling points to separate ethanol (bp 78.4°C) from water (bp 100°C) in the fermented wash to concentrate the product.
A constant-boiling mixture of ethanol and water (95.6% ethanol: 4.4% water) that cannot be separated further by simple distillation. Dehydration requires molecular sieves or azeotropic distillation.
The inhibition of fermentation by oxygen, observed by Louis Pasteur. In aerobic conditions, yeast uses aerobic respiration; in anaerobic conditions, it switches to fermentation for energy.
Ethanol produced by biological fermentation of biomass (sugarcane, corn, cellulose) used as a renewable fuel. Blended with petrol (E5–E20) to reduce fossil fuel dependence and GHG emissions.

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide — a crucial electron carrier coenzyme. NAD⁺ (oxidised) accepts electrons in glycolysis to form NADH. In fermentation, NADH is re-oxidised back to NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue.
Ethanol with ≥99.5% purity (virtually water-free), produced by molecular sieve dehydration. Required for fuel-grade ethanol to prevent engine corrosion and phase separation when blended with petrol.

superbug_bioremediation_bioweapons.html.title: Superbug, Bioremediation & Bioweapons
kp: Superbug (Chakrabarty): Pseudomonas with CAM, OCT, XYL and NAH plasmids; degrades crude oil.
Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980): first patent on a living, engineered organism.
Bioremediation = biological clean-up: biostimulation, bioaugmentation, phytoremediation.
In situ (at site) versus ex situ (excavated).
Exxon Valdez 1989: fertiliser biostimulation accelerated degradation.
Medical "superbugs" (MRSA, NDM-1) are antibiotic-resistant pathogens — a different meaning.
BWC (1975) bans development, production, stockpiling; Geneva Protocol (1925) bans use.
CDC Category A agents: anthrax, smallpox, plague, botulism, tularaemia, haemorrhagic fevers.

sa.q: What is a superbug? Who developed it?
sa.a: A genetically engineered Pseudomonas carrying plasmids (CAM, OCT, XYL, NAH) for degrading different hydrocarbons, developed by A. M. Chakrabarty (General Electric) and patented after the US Supreme Court decision of 1980.

sa.q: Define bioremediation. Distinguish biostimulation and bioaugmentation.
sa.a: Bioremediation is the use of living organisms to degrade or detoxify pollutants. Biostimulation adds nutrients/oxygen to stimulate native microbes; bioaugmentation adds specialised microbes.

sa.q: Differentiate in situ and ex situ bioremediation.
sa.a: In situ treats pollutants at the site (bioventing, biosparging); ex situ treats excavated material elsewhere (land farming, biopiles, bioreactors).

sa.q: What are bioweapons? Name two agents.
sa.a: Bioweapons use pathogens or toxins to cause disease. Examples: Bacillus anthracis (anthrax), Yersinia pestis (plague), variola virus, botulinum toxin.

sa.q: Name the international treaty on biological weapons.
sa.a: The Biological Weapons Convention (opened 1972; in force 1975) prohibits development, production and stockpiling of biological and toxin weapons.

gl.d: Engineered oil-degrading bacterium; also a drug-resistant pathogen in medicine.
Use of organisms to clean polluted environments.
Stimulating native microbes by adding nutrients or oxygen.
Adding specialised microbes to a polluted site.
Using plants to remove or degrade pollutants.
Foreign chemical not normally found in nature, e.g. pesticide.
Injecting air below the water table to stimulate aerobic degradation.
Deliberate release of pathogens or toxins to harm populations.
Biological Weapons Convention (in force 1975).
Containment level (BSL-1 to BSL-4) matching the risk of the agent.

transgenic_animal_technology.html.title: Transgenic Animal Technology
kp: Transgene = foreign gene; transgenic animal carries it in the germ line.
Methods: pronuclear microinjection, ES cell-mediated transfer, retroviral vectors, SCNT, CRISPR.
Super mouse (Palmiter and Brinster, 1982): rat GH gene with metallothionein promoter.
Knock-out: gene targeting by homologous recombination in ES cells; neo (positive) and tk (negative) selection.
Coat-colour markers (129 agouti ES cells; C57BL/6 black host) reveal chimerism and germline transmission.
Dolly (1996): SCNT from mammary cell; Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell; 1 of 277 embryos; died 2003.
Bioreactors: mammary-specific promoters; ATryn (goat), alpha-1-antitrypsin (sheep), lactoferrin (cow).
2007 Nobel Prize: Capecchi, Evans, Smithies (gene targeting).

sa.q: Define transgenic animal. Give two examples.
sa.a: A transgenic animal carries a foreign gene (transgene) stably integrated in its genome and transmitted to offspring. Examples: super mouse with rat growth hormone gene; goat producing human antithrombin in milk.

sa.q: Describe pronuclear microinjection.
sa.a: Fertilised eggs are collected from superovulated females; linearised transgene DNA is injected into the male pronucleus; embryos are transferred into pseudopregnant foster mothers; pups are screened by PCR or Southern blotting of tail DNA; founders are bred to establish a line.

sa.q: How is a knock-out mouse produced?
sa.a: A targeting vector containing neoR (inside the homology region) and tk (outside) is introduced into ES cells; positive-negative selection (G418 + ganciclovir) enriches homologous recombinants; selected ES cells are injected into blastocysts to give chimeras; germline transmission yields heterozygotes, which are inter-crossed to obtain homozygous knock-outs.

sa.q: Explain how Dolly was created.
sa.a: A nucleus from a mammary gland cell of a Finn Dorset ewe was fused by electric pulse with an enucleated egg of a Scottish Blackface ewe; the embryo was cultured and implanted into a surrogate ewe. Dolly was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute.

sa.q: What is meant by animals as bioreactors?
sa.a: Transgenic animals that produce recombinant human proteins in milk or other body fluids under tissue-specific promoters, e.g. antithrombin in goat milk and alpha-1-antitrypsin in sheep milk.

sa.q: Mention two ethical issues of transgenic animals.
sa.a: Animal suffering and welfare; ecological risk and gene flow; patenting of life forms.

gl.d: A foreign gene introduced into an organism.
The first transgenic animal of a line.
Female mated with a vasectomised male; her uterus is ready to receive embryos.
Embryonic stem cell: pluripotent cell from the blastocyst inner cell mass.
An animal made of cells from two genetically different embryos.
Exchange between identical DNA sequences, used for gene targeting.
Somatic cell nuclear transfer: transfer of a somatic nucleus into an enucleated egg.
Loss-of-function mutation created in a chosen gene.
Production of pharmaceutical proteins in farm animals or plants.
Recombinase system for conditional (tissue-specific) gene deletion.

vectors_genetic_engineering.html.title: Vectors in Genetic Engineering – Interactive Learning App

gl.d: A DNA molecule (plasmid, phage, or artificial chromosome) used to carry and transfer foreign DNA into a host cell where it can replicate and/or be expressed.
A specific DNA sequence on a vector where replication is initiated. Ensures the vector can replicate autonomously inside the host cell, independent of the chromosomal DNA.
A gene (typically conferring antibiotic resistance) on a vector that allows selection of transformed host cells on selective media. Untransformed cells die; transformed cells survive.
A short DNA sequence on a cloning vector that contains multiple unique restriction enzyme recognition sites. Also called a polylinker; facilitates insertion of foreign DNA at a defined location.
The foreign DNA fragment (gene of interest) that is cloned into the vector. After restriction digestion and ligation, the insert becomes part of the recombinant DNA molecule.
Transfer DNA — the ~25 kb segment of the Ti plasmid that is excised and transferred by Agrobacterium into the plant cell, where it integrates stably into the plant nuclear genome.
A virus that specifically infects bacteria. Used as a cloning vector because it can inject its DNA (along with foreign inserts) into bacterial host cells with high efficiency.
The cell (usually E. coli or plant cells) into which the recombinant vector is introduced. The host provides the cellular machinery needed for vector replication and gene expression.
A screening method in which insertion of foreign DNA into a restriction site within a marker gene disrupts its function, allowing identification of recombinant clones. Used in pBR322 cloning.
Cohesive-end (cos) sites on the lambda phage genome — 12-nt single-stranded overhangs at both ends of the linear DNA. Essential for circularization inside the host and phage DNA packaging.
The process of inserting a DNA fragment into a vector, introducing it into a host cell, and propagating it to produce many identical copies of the DNA fragment.

The process of introducing recombinant plasmid DNA into a competent bacterial host cell. Successfully transformed cells carry the recombinant vector and are identified by selection on antibiotic media.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.title: Diagram Atlas I: Fundamentals & Vectors
kp: Colour code: red medical, green agricultural, white industrial, blue marine.
Type II restriction enzymes cut palindromes; EcoRI gives 5′ sticky ends, SmaI gives blunt ends.
Ligase joins; phosphatase stops self-ligation; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA.
pBR322: 4,361 bp; ampR, tetR, ori, rop; BamHI/SalI in tet, PstI in amp.
Ti plasmid: T-DNA between LB and RB, vir genes act in trans; disarmed vectors carry the gene of interest.
Lambda 48.5 kb: lytic or lysogenic; replacement vectors carry ~20 kb. M13: ssDNA, non-lytic.
Capacity: plasmid ≤10 kb; lambda ≈ 20–23 kb; cosmid 35–45 kb; BAC/PAC 100–300 kb; YAC 200–2,000 kb.
SV40 (5.2 kb) and transposons (Sleeping Beauty, piggyBac) are animal-cell vectors.
Library size: N = ln(1−P) / ln(1−f).

sa.q: Draw and label the cutting of DNA by EcoRI.
sa.a: EcoRI recognises 5′-GAATTC-3′ (palindromic), cuts between G and A on both strands, and leaves 5′ AATT overhangs (sticky ends) that anneal to any other EcoRI-cut DNA.

sa.q: Name four features of an ideal cloning vector.
sa.a: Origin of replication, selectable marker, unique restriction sites (MCS), small size, high copy number, ability to be introduced into the host.

sa.q: Explain insertional inactivation in pBR322.
sa.a: Foreign DNA is inserted in a marker gene (for example BamHI in tet). The recombinant loses that resistance but keeps the other (Amp-R Tet-S), identified by replica plating.

sa.q: Differentiate lytic and lysogenic cycles.
sa.a: Lytic: phage replicates, lyses the cell, releases progeny. Lysogenic: DNA integrates as a prophage, repressed by cI, and replicates with the host until induction.

sa.q: What is a cosmid and why is it useful?
sa.a: A plasmid containing lambda cos sites that can be packaged in vitro; carries 35–45 kb inserts and is useful for genomic libraries.

sa.q: Compare genomic and cDNA libraries.
sa.a: Genomic libraries contain all DNA (introns and regulatory sequences); cDNA libraries contain only exons of genes expressed in the source tissue, made via reverse transcriptase.

sa.q: Why are YACs used for large genomes?
sa.a: They behave as yeast chromosomes (CEN, ARS, TEL) and carry up to 2,000 kb inserts, reducing the number of clones needed.

gl.d: DNA sequence reading the same 5′→3′ on both strands.
Single-stranded overhang left by a staggered cut.
Flush end with no overhang.
Multiple cloning site: cluster of unique restriction sites.
Gene (for example antibiotic resistance) used to select cells carrying the vector.
Phage genome integrated into the host chromosome.
Cohesive end site of lambda used for packaging and circularisation.
Segment of the Ti plasmid transferred to plant cells.
Bacterial artificial chromosome based on the F plasmid.
Yeast artificial chromosome with CEN, ARS and TEL.
DNA copied from mRNA by reverse transcriptase.
Mobile DNA element that moves by cut-and-paste or copy-and-paste.

atlas2_techniques.html.title: Diagram Atlas II: Cloning & Techniques
kp: Cloning: isolate, cut, ligate, transform, select, screen, verify, grow.
Transformation (bacteria), transfection (animal cells), transduction (virus), microinjection, electroporation, liposome fusion.
Selection = survivors only; screening = tell clones apart.
Insertional inactivation: recombinant is Amp-R Tet-S when inserted in tet.
Blue-white: lacZα, X-gal, IPTG; white = recombinant.
Colony hybridisation uses a labelled probe on a membrane lift of colonies.
Sanger: ddNTP terminators; read from shortest to longest fragment.
PCR: denature 94–95, anneal 50–65, extend 72 °C; 2n amplification.
Southern DNA, Northern RNA, Western protein.

sa.q: List the steps of gene cloning.
sa.a: Isolate target DNA and vector; cut with restriction enzyme; ligate; introduce into host; select transformants; screen for recombinants; verify; grow and express.

sa.q: Differentiate transformation, transfection and transduction.
sa.a: Transformation: uptake of naked DNA by bacteria/yeast. Transfection: non-viral DNA into animal cells. Transduction: gene transfer by a virus.

sa.q: Explain blue-white screening.
sa.a: The vector carries lacZα in its MCS. Without insert, α-complementation makes active β-galactosidase which cleaves X-gal to blue. Insert disrupts lacZα, so colonies are white.

sa.q: How does replica plating identify recombinants?
sa.a: Colonies from a master ampicillin plate are replicated on amp + tet. Colonies absent on the second plate have lost tet through insertional inactivation, so they carry inserts.

sa.q: State the principle of Sanger sequencing.
sa.a: DNA polymerase extends a primer; occasional incorporation of ddNTPs (no 3′-OH) terminates chains. Fragments of all lengths are separated by size and the terminal base read.

sa.q: Write the three steps of a PCR cycle with temperatures.
sa.a: Denaturation 94–95 °C; annealing 50–65 °C; extension 72 °C (Taq).

sa.q: Why does DNA migrate to the anode in electrophoresis?
sa.a: The phosphate backbone carries a negative charge, so DNA moves toward the positive electrode; mobility decreases with log of size.

gl.d: Joining DNA ends with ligase.
Cell treated to take up DNA.
Process allowing only vector-containing cells to grow.
Process that identifies cells with insert among survivors.
Transfer of colony pattern from one plate to others.
Chromogenic substrate cleaved by β-galactosidase.
Non-metabolisable inducer of the lac operon.
Dideoxynucleotide that terminates DNA synthesis.
Product of PCR amplification.
Cycle number at which fluorescence crosses threshold in qPCR.
Labelled nucleic acid or antibody used for detection.
Positive electrode.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.title: Diagram Atlas III: Transgenic & Medical
kp: Transgene = promoter + coding sequence + poly(A); microinjection into the male pronucleus.
Knockout: ES cells, neo/tk selection, blastocyst injection, chimera, breed; 1:2:1 in F2.
Dolly (1996): SCNT from an adult mammary cell; 277 fusions gave 1 live lamb.
Animal bioreactors secrete drugs in milk (goat antithrombin, rabbit C1-inhibitor).
Superbug (Chakrabarty): Pseudomonas with 4 plasmids; Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980).
Hybridoma: B cell + HGPRT− myeloma; HAT selects; screen, clone, expand.
-omab, -ximab, -zumab, -umab = murine, chimeric, humanised, human.
Ex vivo vs in vivo gene therapy; CAR-T is ex vivo; oncolytic viruses and suicide genes.
CRISPR: gRNA + Cas9 + NGG PAM; NHEJ vs HDR.
RFLP (co-dominant), RAPD (dominant), STR fingerprinting (forensics).

sa.q: Describe the production of a transgenic mouse.
sa.a: A construct (promoter + gene + poly A) is injected into the male pronucleus of fertilised eggs; embryos are transferred to a pseudopregnant foster; pups are screened by PCR/Southern; founders are bred to confirm germ-line transmission.

sa.q: How is a knockout mouse produced?
sa.a: A targeting vector with a neo cassette replaces an exon in ES cells by homologous recombination; neo and tk selection enriches targeted cells; they are injected into blastocysts to give chimeras; breeding gives heterozygotes and then homozygous knockouts.

sa.q: Explain the cloning of Dolly.
sa.a: A mammary cell from an adult ewe was starved to G0 and fused by electrical pulse with an enucleated egg; the embryo was cultured and transferred to a surrogate; 1 of 277 fusions produced a live lamb in 1996.

sa.q: What is the role of HAT medium?
sa.a: Aminopterin blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis, so cells must use the salvage pathway (HGPRT, TK). HGPRT-minus myeloma cells die; unfused B cells die naturally; only hybrids survive.

sa.q: Differentiate ex vivo and in vivo gene therapy.
sa.a: Ex vivo: patient cells are modified outside the body and returned. In vivo: the gene vector is injected directly into the patient.

sa.q: Write short notes on CRISPR-Cas9.
sa.a: A guide RNA directs Cas9 to a 20-nt target adjacent to an NGG PAM; Cas9 makes a double-strand break; NHEJ gives knockouts and HDR gives precise edits.

sa.q: Distinguish RFLP and RAPD.
sa.a: RFLP detects fragment-length differences using restriction enzymes and a probe (co-dominant, reproducible). RAPD uses random primers in PCR (dominant, quick, less reproducible).

gl.d: A foreign gene inserted into an organism.
First transgenic animal produced.
Embryonic stem cell, pluripotent and from the inner cell mass.
Animal containing cells from two different embryos.
Somatic cell nuclear transfer.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase of the salvage pathway.
Part of an antigen recognised by an antibody.
Treatment performed outside the body on removed cells.
Protospacer adjacent motif needed by Cas9.
Non-homologous end joining; error-prone DNA repair.
Homology-directed repair using a template.
Short tandem repeat used in DNA profiling.

atlas4_culture_society.html.title: Diagram Atlas IV: Culture, HGP & Ethics
kp: Culture conditions: 37 °C, 5% CO₂, pH 7.2–7.4, humid, sterile; serum 5–10%.
Growth curve: lag, log, plateau, decline; subculture in log phase.
Normal cells have a finite life span (Hayflick limit ~50); continuous lines are transformed.
HeLa, CHO, Vero, HEK-293, BHK-21: know origin and use.
Stem cell potency: totipotent > pluripotent > multipotent; iPSCs by Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc.
Artificial skin: cultured keratinocytes on a collagen/fibroblast matrix.
Bioreactors: stirred tank, airlift, hollow fibre, packed bed; batch, fed-batch, perfusion.
Ethanol: pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂ → ethanol; yeast; distillation.
HGP: 1990–2003, 3.1 Gb, ~20 000 genes, ~1.5% coding; BAC vs shotgun.
Patent: novelty, inventive step, industrial application; 20 years in India; RCGM, GEAC, CPCSEA regulate.

sa.q: List the requirements for animal cell culture.
sa.a: Sterile vessel and aseptic technique; basal medium with serum or defined supplements; 37 °C; 5% CO₂ humidified atmosphere; pH 7.2–7.4 (bicarbonate buffer, phenol red indicator).

sa.q: Describe the growth curve of cultured cells.
sa.a: Lag (adaptation), log (exponential growth), plateau (confluence, nutrient limitation) and decline (toxic waste, death). Subculture in log phase.

sa.q: Differentiate primary culture and cell line.
sa.a: Primary culture is taken directly from tissue; once subcultured it becomes a cell line, finite (40–60 doublings) or continuous (immortal, transformed).

sa.q: What are iPS cells?
sa.a: Pluripotent cells made by reprogramming somatic cells with Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc (Yamanaka 2006); patient-specific and avoid embryo destruction.

sa.q: Describe a stirred-tank bioreactor.
sa.a: A vessel with impeller, sparger, probes for pH, dissolved oxygen and temperature, jacket, inlet and harvest ports; mixing and aeration are controlled for suspension cells.

sa.q: Explain how ethanol is produced industrially.
sa.a: Molasses or hydrolysed starch is fermented by S. cerevisiae at 30–35 °C; wash with 7–10% ethanol is distilled to ~95% and dehydrated with molecular sieves.

sa.q: Compare the two approaches to the Human Genome Project.
sa.a: Public: hierarchical BAC mapping then shotgun of each clone. Celera: whole-genome shotgun and computer assembly. Both converged in 2001.

gl.d: Fraction of the surface covered by adherent cells.
Transfer of cells into fresh vessels (subculture).
Finite number of divisions of normal cells.
Stopping of growth when cells touch.
Able to form all three germ layers.
Continuous supply of fresh medium with cell retention.
Device that bubbles gas into a bioreactor.
Set of overlapping DNA clones or reads.
Bacterial artificial chromosome (100–200 kb).
Existing knowledge that may defeat novelty of a patent.
Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, India.
Replace, Reduce, Refine in animal research.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.title: Diagram Atlas V: Bioinformatics
kp: INSDC: GenBank, ENA and DDBJ share data; UniProt (Swiss-Prot reviewed, TrEMBL unreviewed); PDB for structures.
FASTA: > header + sequence; FASTQ adds Phred quality scores.
Homology is yes/no; similarity and identity are percentages.
Needleman–Wunsch = global; Smith–Waterman = local; both use dynamic programming.
PAM and BLOSUM62 are substitution matrices; affine gap penalties.
BLAST: seed words, extension, HSP, bit score, E-value; BLASTN/P/X/TBLASTN/TBLASTX.
Lower E-value means more significant; 1e-5 is a common threshold.
MSA reveals conserved residues; guide trees order progressive alignments.
Protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary; PDB files list ATOM records.
AlphaFold predicts structures with confidence scores (pLDDT).

sa.q: Differentiate primary and secondary databases.
sa.a: Primary databases hold raw data submitted by researchers (GenBank, PDB); secondary databases hold curated or derived information (Swiss-Prot, Pfam, PROSITE, RefSeq).

sa.q: What is FASTA format?
sa.a: A text format with a header line starting with “>” followed by the sequence in one or more lines.

sa.q: Distinguish global and local alignment.
sa.a: Global (Needleman–Wunsch) aligns whole sequences; local (Smith–Waterman) finds the best matching regions.

sa.q: Explain how BLAST works.
sa.a: Query split into words; neighbourhood words found; database scanned for seeds; hits extended into HSPs; scores converted to bit scores and E-values.

sa.q: What does an E-value of 1e–25 mean?
sa.a: Only 1e–25 matches of that score are expected by chance in a database of that size, so the hit is highly significant.

sa.q: Write short notes on the PDB.
sa.a: Archive of experimentally determined 3-D structures (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM) with a 4-character ID; ATOM records give x, y, z coordinates.

sa.q: List applications of bioinformatics.
sa.a: Gene finding, variant calling, phylogenetics, drug design, structure prediction, transcriptomics, breeding and CRISPR guide design.

gl.d: International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration.
Stable identifier for a database record.
Similarity due to common ancestry.
High-scoring segment pair found by BLAST.
Expected number of chance hits with equal or better score.
Normalised alignment score.
Homologous gene separated by speciation.
Homologous gene separated by duplication.
Contiguous assembled sequence from overlapping reads.
Quality value Q = −10 log₁₀ P(error).
Ancestor and all its descendants.
AlphaFold per-residue confidence (0–100).
